summary: Describes the route optimization problem in NEMO Basic Support. All traffic to and from nodes in a mobile network goes through a tunnel between the mobile router and the home agent when away, which adds delay and can cause congestion. This memo states the problem. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: In NEMO Basic Support, traffic to and from a moving network passes through its Home Agent. RFC 4888 explains how that route can add delay, overload links, and complicate communication in nested networks.

questions: what is the nemo route optimization problem
subtitle: Why NEMO Basic Support can send mobile-network traffic along inefficient routes

tldr.problem: NEMO Basic Support sends traffic between a mobile network and its correspondent through a Home Agent, even when a shorter route exists.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4888 describes the resulting delay, tunnel overhead, bottlenecks, and extra problems caused by nested mobile networks and some security policies.
tldr.outcome: The Informational problem statement explains why route optimization may be needed. It does not define an optimization protocol.

today: RFC 4888 is an Informational problem statement published in July 2007. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the document specifies no route-optimization mechanism.

sections.title: The Basic Routing Path
sections.content:
NEMO Basic Support keeps a mobile network reachable by sending its traffic through a bidirectional tunnel between the Mobile Router and its Home Agent. The Home Agent may be far from both the mobile network and the correspondent node.

As a result, packets may travel to the Home Agent and then back toward a nearby destination. RFC 4888 calls this a sub-optimal route and analyzes its effects as a problem statement for route optimization.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic support routes a moving network's traffic through its Home Agent. That path may be longer than a direct route between the two communicating nodes.

sections.title: Delay, Overhead, and Link Load
sections.content:
A longer path can increase delay and use more network resources. This can affect real-time applications and transport protocols whose performance depends on round-trip time.

Tunneling adds an outer IPv6 header to packets. The RFC notes that one additional IPv6 header adds 320 bits; larger packets can also require fragmentation, which adds delay and reduces bandwidth efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending packets through a distant Home Agent can make them slower and larger. Extra packet size can also increase the chance of fragmentation.

sections.title: Bottlenecks and Nested Networks
sections.content:
The Home Agent or its network link can become a bottleneck for traffic from all nodes in a mobile network. Congestion can delay or discard data, and may also delay signaling needed to establish or update tunnels.

When mobile networks are nested, packets may pass through several Home Agents and gain an IPv6 header at each level. The extra routing can also affect communication between nodes inside the same mobile network, even when their direct path does not leave that network.
sections.plainLanguage: A Home Agent or its link may have to carry traffic for many devices. Nested mobile networks can add more tunnels, headers, delay, and possible points of failure.

sections.title: Security Policies and Stalemates
sections.content:
A home network administrator may block traffic from visiting mobile nodes because those nodes would send traffic through the Home Agent tunnel. Such a policy can also prevent a nested mobile router from using another mobile router for Internet access.

The RFC describes a stalemate when a parent mobile router visits one of its child routers and the child's Home Agent is unreachable through that parent. The child cannot establish its tunnel, while the parent cannot complete its own attachment procedure. The document presents these cases as motivation for route optimization, not as a solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Security rules may block a visiting router from sending traffic through a Home Agent. In a nested setup, this can prevent both the parent and child routers from completing their connections.
